quote: In the early days of Pebblesorting civilization, the heaps they made were mostly small, with counts like 23 or 29
content: The "correct" heaps are the primes. 23 and 29 are prime. 91 is 7 × 13, which is why "13!" is a decisive rebuttal. 1957 is 19 × 103, which is why showing heaps of 19 and 103 ends the war. 8 is composite and 7 is prime. So the parable is built on a property that is objective, decidable and independent of Pebblesorter psychology, and its history is one of real discovery, error and correction. As an allegory it depicts moral realism, a fact that exists whether or not you are moved by it. It shows only that knowing a fact doesn't guarantee caring about it. That is the orthogonality thesis, stipulated in the setup; the parable doesn't argue for it.

quote: The Heap Relativists have warned against this project: They say that AIs, not being of the species Pebblesorter sapiens, may form their own culture with entirely different ideas of which heaps are correct or incorrect.
content: The parable puts the author's own position in the mouths of the characters it mocks. The Heap Relativists predict that AIs may come to value different heaps and propose constraining them by force. Apart from the strapped-on bombs, that is the essay's Friendly-AI view. The "common sense" majority who expect a superintelligence to see the right answer are the realists. The satire only works if you already accept that value is relative to the mind that holds it, so it depends on its own conclusion. It also caricatures real relativists such as Harman, Wong and Prinz, none of whom holds that moral progress is a random walk.

quote: Smarter minds equal smarter heaps. Why would that trend break?
content: The rhetorical question has an empirical answer in the systems actually built, and it isn't the intended one. Among language models trained on human data, larger and more capable models generally do better, not worse, on tests of commonsense moral judgment (Hendrycks et al. 2021). That doesn't refute the orthogonality thesis, which is about what is possible, not about what training on human data produces. But the parable implies that capability gives no grip on the values in the training data. That is a claim about the systems that get built, and so far those systems have followed the "trend" the essay ridicules.
